items.stem: The great silver mines at Potosí began producing in 1545, and their output flowed into European treasuries and the world economy. What was the significance of Potosí silver for the Spanish Empire?
options: (A) It ended Spain's need for any colonial labor in the mines or on plantations.
(B) It financed Spanish state power and tied the Americas to the global economy.
(C) It was used only to decorate colonial churches.
(D) It convinced Spain to abandon silver mining entirely and rely on farming instead.
items.explanation: Potosí's silver was the financial engine of Spain's empire: it paid for armies, administration, and the Crown's European ambitions, while drawing the Americas into worldwide trade networks. That is why the mines also demanded so much forced labor.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the mines intensified the demand for labor; they did not end it.
option_explanations.B: Right — silver funded the Spanish state and connected America to the world economy.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — church decoration was trivial next to the fiscal and global significance.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Spain expanded mining; it did not abandon it.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Spain then built an empire on forced labor — the encomienda system — and on silver, above all the great mines at Potosi (1545), whose output flowed into European treasuries and the world economy'

items.stem: Epidemic disease killed enormous numbers of Native people who had no immunity to European illnesses. Which statement best explains how this demographic catastrophe reshaped Spanish colonial labor?
options: (A) It proved that Native peoples were biologically unsuited to agricultural work of any kind.
(B) It led Spain to free all enslaved workers throughout the colonies.
(C) It had no significant effect on how colonial labor was organized or supplied.
(D) It created a labor shortage that pushed Spain to import enslaved Africans.
items.explanation: The encomienda depended on Native workers, and disease destroyed that workforce. With Native labor collapsing — and Las Casas's reforms making it harder to exploit — Spain turned to a new source of coerced workers: enslaved Africans brought in under the asiento monopoly.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the deaths were caused by lack of immunity to disease, not by unsuitability for work.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Spain expanded coerced labor; it did not free workers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the labor shortage was one of the catastrophe's largest consequences.
option_explanations.D: Right — dying Native populations created the shortage that African slavery filled.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — epidemic disease 'killed enormous numbers of Native people who had no immunity'; 'Spain kept the empire but began replacing Native forced labor with enslaved Africans, imported under the asiento system'

items.stem: Historians rely on Las Casas's writings as evidence of Spanish cruelty, but they also know he wrote to persuade the Crown to reform. Which statement best reflects how historians should use his account?
options: (A) It is a Spanish critic's view of the conquest, but its claims must be weighed against his reformist purpose.
(B) It is useless as historical evidence because Las Casas never actually visited the Americas himself.
(C) It should be accepted uncritically because its author was a Catholic priest.
(D) It proves that every single Spaniard living anywhere in the Americas actively and openly opposed the encomienda system.
items.explanation: Good historical practice treats Las Casas as what he was: an eyewitness with an agenda. His account preserves real descriptions of cruelty, but his goal — moving the Crown to act — means historians check his claims against other evidence rather than taking every detail at face value.

option_explanations.A: Right — use the account while accounting for the author's purpose.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Las Casas lived in the Americas for decades; and a persuasive purpose does not make a source useless.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — no source is accepted uncritically, regardless of the author's occupation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — one critic's account cannot prove what every Spaniard thought.

items.fact_source: u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Las Casas and the Valladolid debate are perfect sourcing material: even in the 1500s, Europeans argued about the morality of empire'

items.stem: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 is best described as which of the following?
options: (A) A Spanish military campaign that conquered the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico.
(B) A peaceful negotiation that gave Pueblo leaders permanent seats in the Spanish colonial government.
(C) A coordinated Native uprising under Popé that drove the Spanish from New Mexico for over a decade.
(D) A revolt by Spanish settlers against the Crown's tax policies in New Mexico.
items.explanation: In 1680, Pueblo communities across New Mexico rose together under Popé's leadership, killing colonists and missionaries and driving the Spanish out entirely. Spain did not reestablish control for more than a decade — one of the most successful Native resistances in colonial North America.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the revolt was Native peoples rising against the Spanish, not the reverse.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — it was a violent uprising and expulsion, not a negotiation.
option_explanations.C: Right — coordinated, led by Popé, and it removed the Spanish for over a decade.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the rebels were Pueblo Native peoples, not Spanish settlers.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Pueblo Revolt (1680): 'the coordinated Native uprising under Pope that expelled Spanish colonists and missionaries from New Mexico'

items.stem: Spain had held New Mexico since 1610 through its mission system. Which factor best explains why the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 succeeded in expelling the Spanish entirely instead of being quickly suppressed?
options: (A) The Spanish voluntarily withdrew to concentrate on defending Florida.
(B) French armies invaded New Mexico and defeated the Spanish garrisons there.
(C) Pueblo communities across many villages coordinated under Popé, striking simultaneously.
(D) A European epidemic wiped out the Spanish missionaries in New Mexico before the fighting even began.
items.explanation: The review stresses that the revolt was 'coordinated': Popé organized villages across New Mexico to rise at the same time. Simultaneous attacks left the Spanish unable to concentrate their forces or relieve the missions one by one — coordination turned scattered grievances into an expulsion.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the Spanish were driven out; they did not choose to leave.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — no French army invaded New Mexico in 1680.
option_explanations.C: Right — coordination across villages is what made the revolt succeed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — epidemic disease devastated Native populations; it did not wipe out the missionaries.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Pueblo Revolt (1680): 'the coordinated Native uprising under Pope that expelled Spanish colonists and missionaries from New Mexico'; u2.md §The story — 'Spain held Florida (St. Augustine, 1565) and New Mexico (Santa Fe, 1610) through missions'

items.stem: The Pueblo Revolt is often studied alongside other acts of resistance in the colonial period. As an example of Native resistance to Spanish colonization, the revolt best illustrates which broader pattern?
options: (A) Long-term cooperation between Native peoples and Spanish missionaries throughout New Mexico.
(B) A dispute between rival Spanish colonial governors over authority.
(C) An English-backed plot to seize control of New Mexico.
(D) Sustained Native opposition to coerced labor and mission control in the Spanish colonies.
items.explanation: The revolt was not an isolated outburst. Across the Spanish colonies, Native peoples resisted forced labor, tribute, and mission discipline — sometimes by fleeing, sometimes by rebelling. The Pueblo Revolt is the largest and most successful example of that constant resistance.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the rebels killed missionaries and destroyed churches; this was opposition, not cooperation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the conflict was between Pueblo peoples and the Spanish, not among Spaniards.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — there is no evidence of English involvement; it was a Pueblo-led uprising.
option_explanations.D: Right — the revolt exemplifies the continuous Native resistance to Spanish coercion.

items.fact_source: u2.md §What the exam tests here — 'Resistance from below — Stono, the Pueblo Revolt, and slave codes as cause-and-effect pairs: repression and resistance escalating together'

items.stem: The encomienda was officially justified as an exchange — Native labor and tribute for Christian instruction. Given Las Casas's campaign, the New Laws of 1542, and the eventual shift to enslaved African labor, what does the system's history suggest about that justification?
options: (A) The religious justification covered forced labor that even many Spaniards found indefensible.
(B) The system operated exactly as its defenders described it in their official reports to the Crown.
(C) Native peoples preferred the encomienda to their pre-contact ways of life.
(D) The Catholic Church officially opposed all missionary activity in the colonies.
items.explanation: If the encomienda had truly been a fair exchange of labor for teaching, it would not have produced a crusading critic, reforming laws, and a wholesale switch to a different coerced workforce. The controversy the system generated shows the religious rationale was a cover for exploitation — one that troubled even Spain itself.

option_explanations.A: Right — the protests and reforms reveal the justification as a cover for forced labor.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the campaigns and laws against it prove it did not work as advertised.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — nothing in the record suggests Native peoples preferred it; they resisted it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Church ran the missions; it did not oppose missionary activity.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Encomienda: 'in theory in exchange for Christian instruction'; New Laws 'pushed by Las Casas'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'from encomienda to the New Laws to African slavery'

items.stem: The New Laws of 1542 limited the encomienda but did not end forced Native labor, and Spain soon expanded African slavery instead. What does this outcome best illustrate?
options: (A) That Spanish reformers had no real influence on colonial policy at all.
(B) That the New Laws actually strengthened and expanded the encomienda system.
(C) That dependence on coerced labor outlasted any single reform of the system.
(D) That Native peoples throughout the colonies were fully liberated by the New Laws.
items.explanation: Reform could change the rules, but it could not change the underlying demand: the colonial economy ran on coerced workers. When one source of forced labor was restricted, the system found another — enslaved Africans. The dependence on coercion survived the reform aimed at it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Las Casas's campaign did produce the New Laws; reformers had real influence.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the laws limited the encomienda; they did not expand it.
option_explanations.C: Right — the shift to African slavery shows coerced labor itself continued.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — forced Native labor continued; the laws curbed the system but did not end it.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Las Casas's writings 'helped curb (but not end) Native enslavement'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'coerced labor continues, but who is coerced changes'

items.stem: In this 18th-century casta painting, the child's label reads 'torna atrás' — 'return backwards.' What does this label reveal about the concerns of Spanish colonial society?

stimulus.image_caption: Casta painting labeled 'De español y albina, torna atrás' (From a Spaniard and an albina, a 'return backwards' child), 18th century.

options: (A) That colonial society welcomed racial mixing without any reservation.
(B) That colonial elites feared mixing could reverse a family's whiteness and status.
(C) That casta labels were assigned randomly with no social meaning at all.
(D) That Spanish law strictly forbade Spaniards from forming families with non-Spaniards.
items.explanation: 'Return backwards' treats whiteness as something that can be lost: a child of mixed ancestry is labeled as a step back toward a lower status. The label exposes the anxiety underneath the whole system — that the boundaries of the hierarchy were fragile and needed constant policing.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — a label meaning 'return backwards' shows anxiety about mixing, not acceptance.
option_explanations.B: Right — the label expresses fear that mixing reverses whiteness and status.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the labels were deliberate markers of social rank, not random.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — mixed families obviously existed; the paintings depict them.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: This single canvas gathers sixteen casta paintings, each labeling a different combination of parents and child. What does the existence of such a comprehensive set best indicate about Spanish colonial culture?

stimulus.image_caption: Casta painting containing a complete set of 16 casta combinations (racial classifications in the Spanish colonies), 18th century, oil on canvas.

options: (A) That classifying people by ancestry had become a systematic preoccupation.
(B) That every colonial household in the Americas owned exactly sixteen casta paintings.
(C) That the Spanish Crown had abolished all racial categories entirely.
(D) That casta paintings served as official legal documents in colonial court cases.
items.explanation: A sixteen-panel catalog of ancestry combinations is not casual decoration — it is a system laid out for display. Producing such a complete visual taxonomy shows how deeply the ranking of people by descent had penetrated colonial culture.

option_explanations.A: Right — a sixteen-category visual catalog shows classification as a cultural obsession.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the number sixteen reflects the categories, not household ownership.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the set displays categories; it did not abolish them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — these were cultural objects displaying the hierarchy, not court records.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'Mestizaje and the casta system — racial mixing in Spanish America and the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'
